items.stem: A revision website states: “Infant mortality is usually higher in LICs than in HICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Poor health care, nutrition and sanitation cause more infant deaths.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [1]

items.stem: Students are investigating the sphere of influence of a shopping centre in Dubai. Identify one risk and explain how it could be reduced.
items.answer: Approaching strangers: work in pairs, ask permission, stay in public places.
items.markingKey: 1 mark risk; 1 mark reduction [1]

items.stem: The following refer to a commercial wheat farm in East Anglia, UK. Classify each as an input, a process or an output, and name the type of farming system. A: Drilling seed. B: Fertile soil. C: Straw. D: Ploughing. E: Spraying. F: Combine harvesting.
items.answer: A process; B input; C output; D process; E process; F process. Type: extensive commercial arable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for every two correct classifications; 1 mark farming type [4]

items.stem: Fig. 5.2 shows the mean concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere at Mauna Loa, Hawaii (ppm): 1960: 317, 1970: 326, 1980: 339, 1990: 354, 2000: 370, 2010: 390, 2020: 414. (a) Calculate the mean rate of increase per year between 1960 and 1990. (b) Calculate the percentage increase from 1960 to 2020.
items.answer: (a) 1.23 ppm per year (b) 30.6%

items.stem: Felix argues that the main reason for rapid population growth in LICs is a high birth rate. How far do you agree? Give evidence for and against before reaching a judgement. You may wish to consider: young population; DTM; death rates.
items.answer: For: High fertility (e.g. Niger about 6.7 children per woman) driven by farming needs, cultural factors and limited contraception. Against: The fall in death rates due to medicine, vaccination and clean water created the gap; a young population structure means many future parents (population momentum). Judgement: Growth comes from the gap between births and deaths; falling death rates started it but high birth rates sustain it.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Table 2.3 shows population data for Country P. 1980: total population 36 million, 22% urban. 2000: total population 61 million, 36% urban. 2020: total population 90 million, 47% urban. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in urban population from 1980 to 2020. (b) Describe two problems that rapid urban growth may cause.
items.answer: (a) 435.4% (b) Informal settlements, shortage of housing, water and sanitation, traffic congestion, air pollution, unemployment and informal jobs.

items.stem: Chloe argues that the benefits of TNCs for host countries outweigh the problems. How far do you agree? Give evidence for and against before reaching a judgement. You may wish to consider: profits; jobs and wages; working conditions.
items.answer: For: TNCs bring jobs, wages, skills, infrastructure and export earnings (e.g. Samsung in Vietnam); the multiplier effect helps local firms. Against: Low wages and poor conditions (Rana Plaza 2013); profit leakage; pollution; dependence on footloose investment. Judgement: For many NEEs the benefits have outweighed the problems, provided governments regulate working conditions and the environment.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: In a questionnaire, 40 shoppers answered one question. Results: car 1, bus 5, walk 26, bicycle 7, train 1. (a) Calculate the percentage for each category. (b) Calculate the angle for each sector of a pie chart. (c) Describe how to draw the pie chart accurately.
items.answer: (a) car 2.5%; bus 12.5%; walk 65%; bicycle 17.5%; train 2.5% (b) car 9°; bus 45°; walk 234°; bicycle 63°; train 9° (c) Draw a circle and a radius from the centre to 12 o’clock; measure each angle clockwise with a protractor, largest first; label or shade each sector with a key and add a title.
items.markingKey: (a) count ÷ 40 × 100 [2] (b) count ÷ 40 × 360; check total 360° [2] (c) 1 mark method; 1 mark labelling [2]

items.stem: Table 4.1 shows the average daily calorie intake per person in four countries. Country S: 2 000 kcal. Country T: 3 600 kcal. Country Q: 2 800 kcal. Country P: 2 600 kcal. The recommended average intake is 2 300 kcal per person per day. (a) Identify the countries with an intake below the recommended level. (b) Calculate the shortfall of the lowest country as a percentage of the recommended intake. (c) Calculate the mean calorie intake of the four countries.
items.answer: (a) Country S (b) 13% below (c) 2750 kcal

items.stem: Fig. 5.3 shows recycling rates of household waste in a city: 2010 15%, 2014 24%, 2018 33%, 2022 41%. In 2014 the city introduced separate bins for paper, glass and food waste and a charge for each bag of non-recycled rubbish. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the recycling rate between 2010 and 2022. (b) Explain how the measures introduced in 2014 may have increased recycling.
items.answer: (a) 173.3% (b) Separate bins made recycling easy; the charge on general rubbish gave a financial incentive to recycle.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “A hamlet has more services than a town.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Hamlets are low in the hierarchy with very few or no services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [1]

items.stem: Fig. 4.3 shows international tourist arrivals (thousands) to a coastal resort in South-east Asia: 2000: 252, 2005: 292, 2010: 375, 2015: 520, 2020: 123, 2023: 587. Tourists spend an average of US$400 each; about 50% of this leaves the country (leakage). Calculate the percentage change in arrivals from 2015 to 2020.

Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “Pollution only affects the place where it is produced.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “The greenhouse effect is entirely harmful.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Air pollution, acid rain and greenhouse gases cross borders; river pollution flows downstream. (b) Not correct. The natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth about 33 °C warmer and habitable; the problem is its enhancement by human activity.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A student calculated Spearman’s rank correlation for distance from the car park (×10 m) (X) and litter count (Y) at 6 sites: X 20, Y 103; X 25, Y 90; X 12, Y 75; X 2, Y 45; X 6, Y 69; X 4, Y 72. (a) Interpret the value of rs. (b) Explain why a scatter graph should be drawn as well as calculating rs.
items.answer: (a) A strong positive correlation. (b) It shows the pattern visually, reveals anomalies and whether the relationship is linear, which a single number can hide.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark strength; 1 mark direction [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that aid is the most effective way to reduce the development gap.
items.answer: For: Emergency and long-term aid can fund health, education and infrastructure; debt relief frees money for services. Against: Fair trade, investment by TNCs, good governance and microfinance can be more sustainable; aid may be misused or create dependency. Judgement: Aid helps most when targeted and combined with fair trade and investment; on its own it is rarely enough.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Country R has a population of 30 million, a birth rate of 15 per 1000 and a death rate of 8 per 1000. In one year 243 000 people immigrated and 158 000 emigrated. (a) Calculate the net migration. (b) Calculate the natural increase in number of people for the year. (c) Calculate the total population change for the year. (d) State whether migration or natural increase contributed more to population change.
With reference to Dharavi, Mumbai, India, or another example of an informal settlement in an LIC or MIC city you have studied, evaluate attempts to improve the settlement.
items.answer: Model answer (Dharavi, Mumbai, India): The Dharavi Redevelopment Project plans to rehouse residents in high-rise blocks with free flats for eligible families and to build commercial space; critics fear loss of businesses and community ties, and many residents are not eligible.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Named schemes (upgrading, rehousing, self-help), what has worked and what has not, judgement. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: Farm A grows 10 tonnes of maize on 5 hectares without irrigation. Farm C grows 10.5 tonnes on 1.5 hectares using irrigation, high-yielding seeds and fertiliser. (a) Calculate the yield per hectare for each farm. (b) Calculate the percentage by which the yield of Farm C is greater than that of Farm A. (c) Suggest two problems Farm C might face from using these methods.
items.answer: (a) Farm A: 2 t/ha; Farm C: 7 t/ha (b) 250% (c) High costs and debt; fertiliser and pesticide pollution of water; salinisation from irrigation; lowering of the water table.
items.markingKey: (a) tonnes ÷ hectares [2] (b) (7 − 2) ÷ 2 × 100 [2] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Name one example of an energy supply scheme you have studied and, for that example, evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of the energy scheme.
items.answer: wind power in Denmark: Benefits: renewable, low carbon, jobs in manufacturing, energy security. Problems: variable output requires links to neighbouring grids and storage; visual impact; offshore farms are expensive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Economic, social and environmental benefits and costs, judgement. [3]

items.stem: In a questionnaire, 50 shoppers answered one question. Results: food 22, clothes 9, services 4, leisure 15. (a) Calculate the angle for each sector of a pie chart. (b) Suggest an alternative way of presenting these results.
items.answer: (a) food 158.4°; clothes 64.8°; services 28.8°; leisure 108° (b) A bar graph or divided bar graph, which is easier to draw and compare accurately.
items.markingKey: (a) count ÷ 50 × 360; check total 360° [2] (b) 1 mark technique; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “Urban problems only occur in LIC cities.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why air pollution is a serious problem in many LIC and MIC cities.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. HIC cities also have congestion, pollution, housing shortages and inequality. (b) Rapid growth in old, poorly maintained vehicles; factories with few controls; burning of waste and fuels for cooking; weak enforcement; in some cities the relief traps smog.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Country B has a population of 15 million. Its farmland can produce enough food for 3 million people and its water supply can support 10 million people. Suggest two ways the country could support more people without reducing the population.
items.answer: Importing food; irrigation and higher-yielding crops; desalination or water recycling; reducing waste; trade using other resources.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Aid can sometimes increase dependency.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Long-term aid may discourage local production or tie countries to donors’ goods and policies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [1]

items.stem: A student tested the hypothesis “Pedestrian numbers decrease with distance from the centre of the CBD.” Results: distance from the CBD 1, 38; distance from the CBD 100, 30; distance from the CBD 150, 28; distance from the CBD 4, 23; distance from the CBD 5, 13; distance from the CBD 6, 4; distance from the CBD 700, 29; distance from the CBD 800, 2 (units: m and pedestrians per 10 minutes). (a) Identify the anomaly and suggest a reason for it. (b) State a conclusion about the hypothesis. Use data to support your answer.
items.answer: (a) (700, 29): possibly a measurement or recording error, or a local factor (e.g. a shop entrance, tributary, path junction or groyne) at that site. (b) Largely supported: 38 at the first site and 2 at the last, apart from the anomaly.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark anomaly; 1 mark plausible reason [2] (b) 1 mark judgement; 1 mark supporting data [2]

items.stem: Name an example of an industrial zone or high-technology industry. For your chosen example, describe the impacts of the industry on the local area.
items.answer: Model answer (Bengaluru, India (information technology)): Hundreds of thousands of IT jobs and firms such as Infosys and Wipro; a growing middle class; but traffic congestion, water shortages, rising house prices and growth of informal settlements.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Jobs, multiplier effect, congestion, housing, environment. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: Table 5.1 shows water use by sector (%) and domestic water use per person per day. Country P: domestic 14%, industry 49%, agriculture 37%, 190 litres per person per day. Country S: domestic 14%, industry 40%, agriculture 46%, 243 litres per person per day. Country T: domestic 12%, industry 8%, agriculture 80%, 32 litres per person per day. (a) Check that the sectors for each country add up to 100%, and state the largest water-using sector in each country. (b) Calculate how many times more water per person per day is used in the highest-use country than the lowest. (c) Suggest why industry uses a larger share of water in richer countries.
items.answer: (a) Each totals 100%; Country P: industry; Country S: agriculture; Country T: agriculture. (b) 7.6 times (c) More manufacturing, power stations (cooling) and processing; farming is a smaller share of the economy and often more efficient.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark check; 1 mark sectors [2] (b) 243 ÷ 32 [1] (c) 1 mark each up to [2]

items.stem: Students carried out a transect from the centre of Santiago to its edge. Table 2.2 shows land value ($ per m²) and the mean height of buildings (storeys). 0 km: $4500, 24 storeys. 1 km: $2700, 7 storeys. 2 km: $1720, 5 storeys. 3 km: $910, 2 storeys. 4 km: $900, 2 storeys. 6 km: $180, 2 storeys. 8 km: $140, 1 storey. (a) Describe how land value changes with distance from the centre. (b) Calculate the percentage fall in land value between 0 km and 2 km. (c) State the first distance at which land value is half or less of the value at the centre.
items.answer: (a) Land value falls rapidly from $4500 at the centre to $910 at 3 km, then more slowly to $140 at 8 km. (b) 61.8% (c) 2 km ($1720)
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark trend; 1 mark change in rate; 1 mark data [3] (b) (4500 − 1720) ÷ 4500 × 100 = 61.8% [2] (c) half of 4500 = 2250 [1]

items.stem: Fig. 1.2 is a population pyramid for Country Q. It shows that 23% of the population is aged 0-14, 68% is aged 15-64 and 9% is aged 65 and over. (a) Calculate the dependency ratio. (b) Describe the likely shape of the pyramid. (c) Explain one problem this population structure may cause.
items.answer: (a) 47.1 (b) Base narrowing, wider in the middle ages, small but growing top. (c) Need to create jobs for a large working-age population; future ageing.
items.markingKey: (a) (23 + 9) ÷ 68 × 100 = 47.1 [2] (b) [2] (c) 1 mark problem; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: Fig. 3.1 shows how the US$80 price of a pair of trainers made in Vietnam is shared: retailer 40%, brand (TNC) profit and marketing 25%, materials 12%, transport and taxes 10%, factory workers’ wages 13%. (a) Calculate the amount paid to factory workers. (b) Calculate how many times more the retailer receives than the factory workers. (c) Suggest why so little of the price goes to the workers.
items.answer: (a) US$10.4 (b) 3.1 times (c) Labour is cheap and plentiful in Vietnam; workers have little bargaining power; most value is added by design, branding and retailing in HICs.

items.stem: Students are investigating the sphere of influence of a shopping centre in Dubai. (a) Identify one risk and explain how it could be reduced. (b) Suggest how the results could be presented.
items.answer: (a) Approaching strangers: work in pairs, ask permission, stay in public places. (b) A desire-line map and a histogram of distances travelled.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark risk; 1 mark reduction [2] (b) 1 mark technique; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A revision website states: “If a result does not fit the pattern it should always be deleted.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “A strong correlation proves that one variable causes the other.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Anomalies should be checked and explained; deleting them without reason can bias the conclusion. (b) Not correct. Correlation shows a relationship; another factor could cause both.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 5.1 shows the sources of electricity generated in Country Q in one year (total 60 TWh): coal 10%, nuclear 25%, oil 30%, solar 5%, natural gas 30%. (a) Calculate the percentage of electricity from renewable sources. (b) Calculate the angle of the solar sector of a pie chart.
items.markingKey: (a) sum of HEP, wind, solar [1] (b) 5 × 3.6 [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “The dependency ratio assumes that everyone aged 15-64 is working.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. In reality some are students, unemployed or caring, and many over 65 work, so it is only an estimate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: For rice farming in the Ganges delta, Bangladesh or another example of a farming system, briefly describe the inputs, processes and outputs of the farming system.
items.answer: rice farming in the Ganges delta, Bangladesh: Inputs: monsoon rain (over 2000 mm), high temperatures, flat alluvial soils renewed by floods, family labour, buffalo, seed; processes: ploughing, flooding paddy fields, transplanting seedlings by hand, weeding, harvesting; outputs: two or three rice crops a year, mostly eaten by the family, with some sold; intensive subsistence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Physical and human inputs, processes, outputs, classification of the system. [4]

items.stem: Fig. 2.1 describes part of a 1:50 000 map. Town M lies at a point where a river is crossed by two main roads; the old centre is on a low hill 20 m above the flood plain; a castle stands on the hill. The river is narrow here and is crossed by an old stone bridge. Railway and roads follow the valley through a gap in a ridge to the north. (a) Identify three site or situation factors that helped the town to grow. (b) Explain why the town has a larger sphere of influence than nearby villages.
items.answer: (a) Any three: defensive hill with castle; dry-point site above flood plain; bridging point; route centre where roads meet; gap through the ridge; water supply from the river. (b) It has more high-order services (supermarkets, secondary school, hospital) and good road links, so people travel further to use it.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [3] (b) 1 mark services; 1 mark accessibility [2]

items.stem: In Country Q, 56% of workers are employed in the primary sector and 14% in the secondary sector. The rest work in the tertiary (and quaternary) sector. (a) Calculate the percentage employed in the tertiary sector. (b) Explain how the employment structure may change in the next 30 years. (c) Describe how these data would be plotted on a triangular graph.
items.answer: (a) 30% (b) Primary share will fall as farming is mechanised and people move to cities; secondary and tertiary will grow with industrialisation and investment. (c) Each side is a 0-100% scale for one sector; read primary, secondary and tertiary along their gridlines; the point where the three lines meet is plotted.
items.markingKey: (a) 100 − 56 − 14 = 30% [1] (b) 1 mark change; 1 mark reason [2] (c) 1 mark three axes; 1 mark plotting point [2]

items.stem: Students are investigating the sphere of influence of a shopping centre in Kuala Lumpur. Diego’s group has one day for fieldwork and their hypothesis is “Most shoppers travel less than 5 km to the shopping centre.” (a) Explain why a pilot study would be useful. (b) Identify two risks and explain how each would be managed.
items.answer: (a) To check that methods work, that questions or recording sheets are clear, and how long each site takes, so the day is used efficiently. (b) Approaching strangers: work in pairs, ask permission, stay in public places; also weather: check forecast and carry suitable clothing.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [2] (b) 1 mark each risk; 1 mark each management [4]

items.stem: Fig. 5.2 shows the mean concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere at Mauna Loa, Hawaii (ppm): 1960: 317, 1970: 326, 1980: 339, 1990: 354, 2000: 370, 2010: 390, 2020: 414. (a) Calculate the mean rate of increase per year between 1960 and 1990. (b) Calculate the percentage increase from 1960 to 2020. (c) Suggest why Mauna Loa is a good place to measure CO₂.
items.answer: (a) 1.23 ppm per year (b) 30.6% (c) It is remote and high, far from local sources of pollution, so readings represent the global atmosphere.

items.stem: Study Fig. 1.3, a choropleth map of Brazil. Density is highest along the south-east coast (over 100 per km²), lower in the central plateau, and lowest in the Amazon rainforest (under 5 per km²). (a) Suggest physical reasons why the Amazon basin is sparsely populated. (b) Identify one disadvantage of a choropleth map for showing population density.
items.answer: (a) Dense rainforest, hot humid climate, infertile soils, flooding and disease. (b) It suggests density is the same across each whole area and changes suddenly at boundaries.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: A company wants to build a steel works. Fig. 4.2 describes three possible sites. Site A: next to a motorway junction on the edge of a city, flat greenfield land, 10 km from a university. Site B: beside a deep-water port with rail links, on cheap reclaimed land far from housing. Site C: in the city centre on a small brownfield plot with narrow streets and high land values. (a) Explain why Site C would be unsuitable. (b) Suggest how local people might react to the new factory.
items.answer: (a) Small plot with no room to expand; expensive land; congestion in narrow streets makes deliveries slow. (b) Support: new jobs and income, multiplier effect. Oppose: noise, traffic, pollution, loss of open land.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [2] (b) 1 mark each side [2]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Recycling uses no energy at all.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Collecting and processing materials uses energy, though usually less than making new products.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [3]

items.stem: In Country P, 27% of workers are employed in the primary sector and 29% in the secondary sector. The rest work in the tertiary (and quaternary) sector. (a) Calculate the percentage employed in the tertiary sector. (b) The workforce is 12 million. Calculate how many people work in the primary sector.
items.answer: (a) 44% (b) 3.24 million

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Rural-urban fringe land is often used for retail parks and business parks.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Land is cheaper, there is space for parking and good access to main roads.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: An island state has a population of 12 million. Its farmland can produce enough food for 12 million people and its water supply can support 5 million people. (a) Identify the resource that limits the population most. (b) Calculate the surplus or shortfall in people supported by food. (c) Suggest two ways the country could support more people without reducing the population.
items.answer: (a) Water (b) surplus of 0 million (c) Importing food; irrigation and higher-yielding crops; desalination or water recycling; reducing waste; trade using other resources.
items.markingKey: (a) Smaller of 12 and 5 million [1] (b) 12 − 12 [1] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Students are investigating how a river changes downstream near Mumbai. Freya’s group has one day for fieldwork and their hypothesis is “The width, depth and velocity of the river increase with distance downstream.” (a) Explain why a pilot study would be useful. (b) Explain how the group could make sure their results are reliable.
items.answer: (a) To check that methods work, that questions or recording sheets are clear, and how long each site takes, so the day is used efficiently. (b) Repeat measurements and take means, use the same equipment and times at each site, use a large enough sample, and have the same person record each measurement.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [2] (b) 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Farm A grows 5 tonnes of potatoes on 2 hectares without irrigation. Farm C grows 17.5 tonnes on 2.5 hectares using irrigation, high-yielding seeds and fertiliser. (a) Calculate the percentage by which the yield of Farm C is greater than that of Farm A. (b) Explain why Farm C has a higher yield.
items.answer: (a) 180% (b) Irrigation provides reliable water; high-yielding varieties produce more grain; fertiliser adds nutrients – this is intensive, capital-based farming.
items.markingKey: (a) (7 − 2.5) ÷ 2.5 × 100 [2] (b) 1 mark each input explained up to [3]

items.stem: Using a case study of a water supply scheme, such as the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, evaluate the success of the scheme.
items.answer: Model answer (the Lesotho Highlands Water Project): Benefits: reliable water for about 12 million people in South Africa; royalties of millions of US$ a year and electricity for Lesotho. Problems: thousands of people relocated and farmland flooded; reduced flow downstream; corruption scandals; many rural Basotho still lack piped water.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Economic, social and environmental advantages and disadvantages; judgement. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: Table 3.2 shows mean income per person (US$) and adult literacy (%) by region in Country P. North: $7 000, 82%. North-east: $4 000, 78%. Centre: $10 000, 94%. South-east: $15 000, 96%. South: $13 000, 94%. (a) Calculate how many times greater income is in the richest region than the poorest. (b) Suggest why the core region is wealthier. (c) Suggest two ways the government could reduce the inequality.
items.answer: (a) 3.8 times (b) Ports, industry and services concentrated there; investment by TNCs and government; better infrastructure and education attract more investment (cumulative causation). (c) Invest in roads, schools and health in poorer regions; tax incentives for firms to locate there; new capital or growth poles; cash-transfer schemes.
items.markingKey: (a) 15 000 ÷ 4 000 [1] (b) 1 mark each up to [3] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Table 2.3 shows population data for Country R. 1980: total population 30 million, 21% urban. 2000: total population 53 million, 33% urban. 2020: total population 74 million, 42% urban. (a) Explain the difference between urbanisation and urban growth, using the data. (b) Suggest two reasons for the changes shown.
items.answer: (a) Urbanisation is the rise in the urban share (21% to 42%); urban growth is the rise in the number of urban people (6.3 to 31.1 million). (b) Rural-urban migration (push: poverty, lack of services; pull: jobs, services) and high natural increase in cities.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each with data [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Table 1.2 shows the population structure of Country Y (% of total population). 0-14: males 5%, females 4%. 15-29: males 4%, females 5%. 30-44: males 5%, females 6%. 45-59: males 11%, females 10%. 60-74: males 10%, females 10%. 75+: males 6%, females 24%. (a) Calculate the percentage of the population aged 0-14. (b) Calculate the percentage aged 60 and over. (c) Compare the number of elderly males and females, and suggest a reason.
items.answer: (a) 9% (b) 50% (c) More elderly women than men: women have a higher life expectancy.
items.markingKey: (a) 5 + 4 = 9% [1] (b) 10 + 10 + 6 + 24 = 50% [1] (c) 1 mark comparison; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Explain why the functions of many villages have changed.
items.answer: Farming employs fewer people; commuters and retired people have moved in; second homes and tourism; services such as shops and post offices have closed because of car ownership and online shopping.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Table 1.2 shows the population structure of Country X (% of total population). 0-14: males 12%, females 11%. 15-29: males 12%, females 13%. 30-44: males 7%, females 8%. 45-59: males 5%, females 4%. 60-74: males 11%, females 11%. 75+: males 4%, females 2%. Compare the number of elderly males and females, and suggest a reason.
items.answer: More elderly men than women here, which is unusual; it may reflect migration or the effects of rounding.
items.markingKey: 1 mark comparison; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Food aid is useful in emergencies but can harm local farmers if it continues for too long.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Free food can lower local prices and discourage farmers from producing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: In Country R, 33% of workers are employed in the primary sector and 35% in the secondary sector. The rest work in the tertiary (and quaternary) sector. (a) Explain how the employment structure may change in the next 30 years. (b) Describe how these data would be plotted on a triangular graph.
items.answer: (a) Secondary may peak then fall as wages rise and automation increases; tertiary and quaternary will grow. (b) Each side is a 0-100% scale for one sector; read primary, secondary and tertiary along their gridlines; the point where the three lines meet is plotted.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark change; 1 mark reason [2] (b) 1 mark three axes; 1 mark plotting point [2]

items.stem: Students are investigating how beach sediment changes along a beach affected by longshore drift near Hanoi. Lina’s group tested the hypothesis “Pebbles become smaller and more rounded in the direction of longshore drift.” using measuring the long axis of 10 pebbles at each site with callipers and classifying roundness using a Powers scale. In their evaluation they note that data were collected on one afternoon only and a sample of 12 people was used. (a) Suggest improvements to the investigation. (b) Suggest one further investigation that would extend this enquiry.
items.answer: (a) Collect data on several days and times; use more sites and larger samples; repeat readings and use means; the same person and equipment at each site; avoid bad weather or record it. (b) Repeat in a different season or place; add another variable (e.g. compare with another river/town); use secondary data to compare with past years.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each improvement up to [3] (b) 1 mark suggestion; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Fig. 5.1 shows the sources of electricity generated in Country Q in one year (total 60 TWh): oil 15%, hydro-electric 30%, solar 10%, wind 15%, nuclear 30%. (a) Calculate the percentage of electricity from renewable sources. (b) Calculate how much electricity (TWh) came from oil. (c) Calculate the angle of the oil sector of a pie chart. (d) Explain one disadvantage of relying heavily on wind and solar power.
items.answer: (a) 55% (b) 9 TWh (c) 54° (d) Output varies with weather and time of day, so backup power or storage is needed.
items.markingKey: (a) sum of HEP, wind, solar [1] (b) 15% × 60 [1] (c) 15 × 3.6 [1] (d) 1 mark problem; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: “Anti-natalist policies are the most effective way of reducing rapid population growth.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Support your answer with examples. You may wish to consider: human rights; China; contraception.
items.answer: For: China’s one-child policy cut fertility quickly. Against: Education of women, better health care (lower infant mortality) and economic development reduce birth rates voluntarily and without abuses, e.g. Kerala, Bangladesh. Coercive policies cause gender imbalance and ageing. Judgement: Development and education are usually more effective and sustainable than strict policies, though family planning programmes help.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Table 2.3 shows population data for Country P. 1980: total population 26 million, 28% urban. 2000: total population 44 million, 42% urban. 2020: total population 63 million, 51% urban. (a) Calculate the urban population in 1980 and in 2020. (b) Suggest two reasons for the changes shown. (c) Describe two problems that rapid urban growth may cause.
items.answer: (a) 1980: 7.3 million; 2020: 32.1 million (b) Rural-urban migration (push: poverty, lack of services; pull: jobs, services) and high natural increase in cities. (c) Informal settlements, shortage of housing, water and sanitation, traffic congestion, air pollution, unemployment and informal jobs.
items.markingKey: (a) 26 × 28% and 63 × 51% [2] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Table 1.3 shows the population and area of regions in a country. Region A: population 3 100 000, area 10 000 km². Region B: population 1 100 000, area 88 000 km². Region C: population 6 100 000, area 15 000 km². Region D: population 20 000, area 253 000 km². (a) Identify the most densely and the most sparsely populated regions. (b) Suggest physical factors that might explain the low density in Region D.
items.answer: (a) Densest: Region C; sparsest: Region D (b) Mountains or steep slopes; desert or very cold climate; poor soils; dense forest; lack of water.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each up to [2]

items.stem: For the Maldives or another example of tourism in an area, briefly explain the problems caused by tourism.
items.answer: the Maldives: Damage to coral reefs; waste disposed of at Thilafushi “rubbish island”; dependence on tourism; leakage to foreign-owned resorts; vulnerability to sea-level rise.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Environmental, social and economic problems. [4]
